q-108309.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line in Vector Form and a Plane in Dot Product Form
q-108309.source_problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨2,3,-1⟩+t⟨-1,2,3⟩,\,Π:r\cdot ⟨-2,1,4⟩=11.
$$
q-108309.worked_solution:
Let's write the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨2-t,3+2t,-1+3t⟩.
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨2-t,3+2t,-1+3t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-2,1,4⟩ & =11 \\ ⟨2-t,3+2t,-1+3t⟩\cdot ⟨-2,1,4⟩ & =11 \\ -2(2-t)+1(3+2t)+4(-1+3t) & =11 \\ -4+2t+3+2t-4+12t & =11 \\ 16t & =16 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$ is obtained by substituting $t=1$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2-1,3+2(1),-1+3(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,5,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(1,5,2).$

$$

q-108326.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line in Parametric Form and a Plane in Cartesian Form

q-108368.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line in Parametric Form and a Plane in Cartesian Form

q-108371.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line and a Plane Given in Other Forms
q-108371.source_problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨4,-2,3⟩+w⟨5,-1,2⟩,\,Π:r=⟨10,-5,12⟩+s⟨4,3,0⟩+t⟨0,2,5⟩.
$$
q-108371.worked_solution:
From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vector to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨4,3,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,5⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =15i-20j+8k \\  & =⟨15,-20,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ & =⟨10,-5,12⟩\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ & =346.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨4,-2,3⟩+w⟨5,-1,2⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ & =346 \\ ⟨4+5w,-2-w,3+2w⟩\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ & =346 \\ 15(4+5w)-20(-2-w)+8(3+2w) & =346 \\ 60+75w+40+20w+24+16w & =346 \\ 111w & =222 \\ w & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨4+5(2),-2-(2),3+2(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨14,-4,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(14,-4,7).$

q-108889.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line and a Plane Given in Other Forms
q-108889.source_problem:

l:\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3},\,Π:r\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩=39.
$$
q-108889.worked_solution:
From the equation of the line $l$, we know that it passes through the point $A(3,1,-4)$ and it is parallel to the vector $v=⟨5,2,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨3,1,-4⟩+t⟨5,2,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩ & =39 \\ ⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩ & =39 \\ (-3)(3+5t)+2(1+2t)-(-4+3t) & =39 \\ -9-15t+2+4t+4-3t & =39 \\ -14t & =42 \\ t & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-3$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨3+5(-3),1+2(-3),-4+3(-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-5,-13⟩.\end{aligned}

So, we get $P(-12,-5,-13).$

q-109158.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy.
$$
q-109158.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{{y}^{-1}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x}\,⇒\,y=\frac{3x}{C-{x}^{3}}\,.
$$

q-109302.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
q-109302.source_problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
q-109302.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-18t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-18t+3) \\  & =12t-18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-18 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{18}{12} \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{3}{2}) & =6{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-18(\frac{3}{2})+3 \\  & =6(\frac{9}{4})-27+3 \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-27+3 \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-109307.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
q-109307.source_problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=7{t}^{2}-{t}^{3},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
q-109307.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}) \\  & =14t-3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(14t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =14-6t\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}14-6t & =0 \\ -6t & =-14 \\ t & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{7}{3}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{7}{3}) & =14(\frac{7}{3})-3{(\frac{7}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{98}{3}-\frac{49}{3} \\  & =\frac{49}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-109639.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
q-109639.source_problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
q-109639.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-5y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=-1,f(t)=-5{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(2-(-1))(-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}) \\  & =3(-5{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}) \\  & =-15{x}_{1}+12{e}^{t}{x}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

q-110078.knowledge_point: Working With Systems Containing Inequalities Presented in Standard Form
q-110078.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996965/assets/3905dacc3977857933a48ced329fc245b357f732aec520e67998efc0b5d7cdab.png)

Which of the following systems of inequalities defines the shaded region shown above?
q-110078.worked_solution:
Consider the line $x+2y=-8.$ Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Writing the equation of this line in slope-intercept form, we have

$$
y=-\frac{1}{2}x-4.
$$

Now, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y\ge -\frac{1}{2}x-4,
$$

    

which we can rewrite as

$$
x+2y\ge -8.
$$

Now consider the line $y=\frac{1}{2}x+1.$ Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies *below* the line, the inequality is a "less than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y\le \frac{1}{2}x+1.
$$

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y\ge -8 \\ y\le \frac{1}{2}x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110754.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection
q-110754.source_problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
q-110754.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}}.
$$

q-110756.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection
q-110756.source_problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 7\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
q-110756.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{3}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
{a}_{3}=1\cdot {a}_{1}+1\cdot {a}_{2}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{3}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ that is to say,

q-112487.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Irrational
q-112487.source_problem: The equation ${m}^{2}+8=-8m$ can be written in the form $(m+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
q-112487.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, the $-8m$ term to the left-hand side, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+8 & =-8m \\ {m}^{2}+8m & =-8 \\ {m}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot m & =-8 \\ {m}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot m+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =-8 \\ (m+4)^{2}-{4}^{2} & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(m+4)^{2}-{4}^{2} & =-8 \\ (m+4)^{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=8,$ and $p+q=12.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(m+4)^{2} & =8 \\ \sqrt{(m+4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{8} \\ |m+4| & =\sqrt{8} \\ m+4 & =\pm 2\sqrt{2} \\ m & =-4\pm 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-112524.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Positive Leading Coefficient
q-112524.source_problem: The equation $4{x}^{2}+6x-5=0$ can be written in the form $4(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q.$
q-112524.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-5 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =5 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{29}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}$ and $q=\frac{29}{4}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{29}{4}=\frac{32}{4}=8.
$$

q-112863.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Roots of a Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
q-112863.source_problem: According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following could be a root of the polynomial $f(x)=7{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+x-14?$
q-112863.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-14,$ and the leading coefficient is $7.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-14}{\text{factor of }7}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $-2=\frac{-2}{1}$ takes the above form since the numerator $(-2)$ is a factor of $-14$ and the denominator $(1)$ is a factor of $7.$

q-113245.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots by Completing the Square
q-113245.source_problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-6x+34=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
q-113245.worked_solution:
We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+34 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-6x & =-34\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x & =-34 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2} & =-34 \\ (x-3)^{2}-9 & =-34 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =-25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-3,\,q=-25,$ and $p+q=-28.$

Finally, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2} & =-25 \\ x-3 & =\pm \sqrt{-25} \\ x-3 & =\pm 5\,\text{i} \\ x & =3\pm 5\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=3+5\,\text{i}$ and $x=3-5\,\text{i}.$

q-116564.knowledge_point: Finding the Asymptotes of a Hyperbola Given Its Equation in Non-Standard Form
q-116564.source_problem: Find the asymptotes of the hyperbola $8{y}^{2}-25{x}^{2}=200.$
q-116564.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.
$$

To rewrite the given equation in standard form, we divide both sides of the equation by $200$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{2}-25{x}^{2} & =200 \\ \frac{8{y}^{2}}{200}-\frac{25{x}^{2}}{200} & =\frac{200}{200} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $a=\sqrt{25}=5,$ and $b=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are $y=\pm \frac{5}{2\sqrt{2}}x=\pm \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{4}x.$

q-118389.knowledge_point: Finding an Equation That Determines a Minimum Distance
q-118389.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068172/assets/37434a61262f829160fc2b19fcadb67745a024d589cd1ce318ca4ab90d6ab2d9.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y=\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}}$ that is closest to the point $(2,0)$ satisfies the equation

$$
2x-3-=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?
q-118389.worked_solution:
Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{(\frac{x+1}{\sqrt{x}})}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+\frac{{x}^{2}+2x+1}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x+2+\frac{1}{x} \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+\frac{1}{x}+6.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-119037.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration
q-119037.source_problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)-6{e}^{-3x}=1.$
q-119037.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1+6{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+6{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+6\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+6(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =x-2{e}^{-3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120778.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
q-120778.source_problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=12-3{t}^{2},$ where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=15\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
q-120778.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 12-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-6(2) \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (12-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =12t-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=15.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12(1)-(1)^{3}+C & =15 \\ 11+C & =15\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4+12t-{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4+12(2)-(2)^{3}=20\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

q-122351.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
q-122351.source_problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
q-122351.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14059489/assets/ee516744d915553bf962b498af522cf0006d42c5d0e0e2a003e6f385dd069e4a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8\sqrt{0+1}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8\sqrt{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =16\sqrt{x+1} \\ v & =\pm 4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4\sqrt[4]{x+1}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4\sqrt[4]{x+1} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{x+1}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{4}{3}(x+1)^{3/4} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{3{C}_{1}}{4}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/4}=3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/4} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{4/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{4/3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

q-122931.knowledge_point: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve
q-122931.source_problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{t},\,y=2t{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
q-122931.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =e, \\ y & =2(1){e}^{1}-2{e}^{1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(e,0).$  For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t{e}^{t}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =2(1)=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,2\,}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(e,0)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =(-\frac{1}{2})(x-e) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{e}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123020.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
q-123020.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039829/assets/ae210abc4028440aa9c822510d68f0ab0b8ba4b9f5806dd299149e953ccd1b21.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-4,\,y=2t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=0$ (shown above)?
q-123020.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-4)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

and

q-123439.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
q-123439.source_problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2\le \theta \le \pi /2$ ?
q-123439.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123458.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
q-123458.source_problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi $ ?
q-123458.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta })^{2}+{(\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )+\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta }{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1-{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}+4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )[1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta +4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123519.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
q-123519.source_problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
q-123519.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}+{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\frac{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(4-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123769.knowledge_point: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation
q-123769.source_problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=3-t,\,\,\,y=t+2,\,t\ge 1,
$$

determine the ranges of $x$ and $y.$
q-123769.worked_solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ note that $3-t\le 2$ for all $t\ge 1.$ Consequently, $x=3-t\le 2.$

- To find the range of $y,$ note that $t+2\ge 3$ for all $t\ge 1.$ Consequently, $y=t+2\ge 3.$

Therefore, the ranges are $x\le 2$ and $y\ge 3.$

q-123773.knowledge_point: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation Defined in Terms of Trigonometric Functions
q-123773.source_problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
q-123773.worked_solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\ge -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \text{ }\ge -1 \\ -1 & \le -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ 1-1 & \le 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1+1 \\ 0 & \le x\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $0\le x\le 2.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -1+2 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\le 1+2 \\ 1 & \le y\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $1\le y\le 3.$

Therefore, the ranges are $0\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3.$

q-123775.knowledge_point: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation Defined in Terms of Trigonometric Functions
q-123775.source_problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
q-123775.worked_solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \le \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \le x\le \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -1+3 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\le 1+3 \\ 2 & \le y\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $2\le y\le 4.$

Therefore, the ranges are $-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}$ and $2\le y\le 4.$

q-123889.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
q-123889.source_problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by the graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}?$
q-123889.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$
